Model - Types

   – Physics-Based Modeling: These are grounded in mathematics, with equations derived
       from basic physical principles (e.g., Newton’s law of gravity).
             •  While they are "first principle" models, they may still have fidelity limitations due to
            assumptions or omitted factors like air resistance.
   –  Finite Element Modeling (FEM): This method decomposes large, complicated objects
         into a set of smaller, simpler "elements" represented by a mesh of nodes.
             •   It is widely used in mechanical and aerospace engineering for structural and fluid
            dynamics analysis.
   – Data-Based Modeling: This approach uses empirical data
       from field experience, testing, or expert knowledge to build a
        model.
             •  AI researchers use this when they train a neural network on
            thousands of hours of real-world driving data to create a
             "black-box" model of human driving behavior.

Simulation - Paradigms
Three prominent paradigms - to model system behavior over time:
1.  Monte Carlo Simulation: Uses random sampling from input distributions to
    calculate outputs, relying on probabilities to model behavior.
     •   Frequently used in AI for Reinforcement Learning. The AI performs thousands
        of random "trials" to learn which actions lead to a reward.
2.  Continuous Simulation: System variables are continuous functions of time,
     typically evolving using differential equations.
     •  Used to model a robot dynamics at every millisecond.
3.  Discrete-Event Simulation: Variables change only at
     distinct points in time associated with specific events
     •   In factory automation, the system state only changes
      when a robot finishes a task or a new part arrives on a
       conveyor belt.
